reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine / European Respiratory Monograph on rare lung disease
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2, encoding a type IIb sodium-phosphate cotransporter in alveolar type II cells
Failure to clear alveolar phosphate leads to deposition of countless calcium-phosphate concretions (microliths, calcospherites) filling the alveolar spaces
Striking clinico-radiological dissociation is characteristic, with extensive calcified change on imaging in a patient who may be minimally symptomatic for years
The chest radiograph classically shows a diffuse fine sand-like micronodular pattern (a 'sandstorm' lung) that is densest in the lower zones
High-resolution CT demonstrates calcified micronodules, subpleural calcific interlobular septal thickening, and dense posterior/basal consolidation, sometimes with a subpleural 'black pleural line'
Diagnosis is often made confidently on imaging in the right context and can be confirmed by identifying microliths in sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or biopsy, or by genetic testing
Familial clustering is common and screening of siblings is worthwhile given the recessive inheritance
There is no proven disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive and lung transplantation is considered for end-stage disease
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2, which encodes the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter normally expressed on alveolar type II pneumocytes. This transporter clears phosphate liberated by the turnover of surfactant phospholipid from the alveolar lining fluid. When it is deficient, phosphate accumulates and combines with calcium to precipitate as innumerable laminated calcium-phosphate microliths within the alveoli. Progressive filling of the air spaces and later interstitial fibrosis and ossification impair gas exchange and lung compliance over decades, eventually producing restrictive physiology and pulmonary hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic pulmonary calcification from chronic renal failure or hypercalcaemia
Miliary tuberculosis or other diffuse micronodular infection
Amiodarone-related or other diffuse calcified deposition
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest to characterise calcified micronodules, septal thickening, and the subpleural black pleural line
Genetic testing for pathogenic SLC34A2 variants and screening of first-degree relatives
Bronchoalveolar lavage or transbronchial biopsy to demonstrate calcospherite microliths when imaging is inconclusive
Pulmonary function tests with diffusing capacity to quantify restriction and gas-transfer impairment
Serum calcium, phosphate, and renal function to exclude metastatic calcification
Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary hypertension in advanced disease
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness and hypoxaemia signalling advancing restrictive disease
Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart strain
Pneumothorax, which can complicate the stiff calcified lung
Rapid functional decline suggesting need for transplant assessment
reference.prognosis: The disease usually progresses very slowly over decades, and many patients remain stable for long periods, but a subset develop relentless restrictive fibrosis, respiratory failure, and pulmonary hypertension for which lung transplantation is the only definitive option.
pitfalls: Mistaking the dramatic calcified imaging for widespread infection such as miliary tuberculosis and treating inappropriately
Assuming severe disease because imaging looks alarming, when symptoms may be mild for years
Overlooking the recessive inheritance and failing to screen affected siblings
Attributing the calcification to renal metabolic disease without checking calcium, phosphate, and renal function
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
European Respiratory Society monograph on rare interstitial lung diseases
management: No established disease-modifying drug therapy exists, so care is largely supportive as the microlith burden accumulates, with bisphosphonates and a low-phosphate diet remaining unproven experimental options
Long-term oxygen therapy for hypoxaemic respiratory failure and pulmonary rehabilitation to support exercise capacity
Serial pulmonary function testing with diffusing capacity and imaging to monitor restrictive progression
Echocardiographic surveillance for pulmonary hypertension in advanced disease, with supportive treatment of right heart failure
Smoking avoidance and prompt treatment of intercurrent respiratory infection
Lung transplantation as the only definitive option for end-stage restrictive fibrosis and respiratory failure
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and screening of first-degree relatives for SLC34A2 variants
